notes.12:2: Hebrew "kilyoteihem" literally means "their kidneys," the biblical idiom for a person's innermost thoughts, conscience, and affections.
notes.12:4: The third-person subject "He" most likely refers to God (echoing "You see me" in v. 3), though some take it to refer to the prophet Jeremiah; Hebrew "aharitenu" means "our end" or "our final outcome."
notes.12:5: Hebrew "tetahareh" is a rare Tiphel form of "harah" meaning "compete with" or "contend against" (also in Jer 22:15). "The thicket of the Jordan" renders "ge'on hayyarden," literally "the pride/swelling of the Jordan," referring to the dense, lion-infested riverbank vegetation.
notes.12:9: Hebrew "ayit tsavua" literally means "a speckled/colored bird of prey," though the exact lexical sense of "tsavua" is debated.
notes.13:4: Hebrew "Perat" normally denotes the Euphrates River, though some scholars identify it here with Parah, a town northeast of Anathoth (Josh 18:23), as a wordplay on the Euphrates.
notes.13:16: Qere reads "weshit" ("and makes it," waw plus an infinitive form continuing the preceding verb), whereas Ketiv reads "yashit" ("He makes it," an imperfect without "and").
notes.13:20: Qere reads masculine plural imperatives ("se'u", "ure'u") agreeing with plural "your eyes," whereas Ketiv reads feminine singular imperatives ("se'i", "ure'i") anticipating the feminine singular address to Jerusalem in the second half of the verse.
notes.13:21: Hebrew "allufim" plays on the double meaning "close companions/allies" and "chiefs/rulers," while the middle clause functions as a parenthetical aside highlighting Judah's own culpability.
notes.13:27: "How much longer still?" renders the compressed Hebrew idiom "aharei matay od," literally "after when yet?"
notes.14:3: Qere reads "tse'ireihem" ("their lowly ones / attendants," contrasting with "their nobles"), whereas Ketiv displays the orthographic variant "ts'wryhm."
notes.14:4: Hebrew "hattah" literally means "is shattered" or "is dismayed," used here of earth cracked by severe drought.
notes.14:9: Hebrew "nidham" is a hapax legomenon (Niphal participle of "daham") meaning "stunned," "astonished," or "taken aback."
notes.14:14: Two Ketiv/Qere morphological variants occur here: Qere reads "we'elil" ("and futility/worthlessness") and "wetarmit" ("and deceit") for Ketiv "w'lwl" and "wtrmwt."
notes.14:18: The closing clause "saharu el-erets welo yada'u" is syntactically compressed and may mean either "go wandering / ply their trade through the land and do not understand" or "wander into a land that they do not know."
notes.15:8: The noun rendered "anguish" (Hebrew ir, distinct from the homonym meaning "city") denotes sudden agitation or terror when paired with behalot ("terrors").
notes.15:10: The clause "every one of them curses me" translates a grammatically blended Masoretic form (mekalelawni, combining participial and verbal suffix elements from the Piel of qalal) following the collective kulloh ("all of it").
notes.15:11: Translates the Qere sheritika (Piel perfect of sharah, "set free, release"); the Ketiv reads shrwtek, variously understood as a verbal noun from the same root or a defective form meaning "your remnant."
notes.15:14: Follows the Masoretic Hiphil of abar ("cause to pass over") with et taken as the preposition "with" and an implied object ("you"); several ancient versions instead reflect the graphically similar root abad ("make to serve"), as in 17:4.
notes.15:16: Translates the Qere singular debarka ("Your word"), agreeing with the singular verb wayehi; the Ketiv reads the plural debareka ("Your words").
notes.16:5: Hebrew bet marzeah ("house of mourning") refers to a ritual funerary banquet held in honor of the dead.
notes.16:7: The Masoretic verb yifresu (Qal of paras, "break [bread]") omits an explicit object ("bread") and is followed by al-ebel ("in mourning"), which some ancient versions read as "bread."
notes.16:16: Translates the Qere dayyagim ("fishermen"), matching the pattern of tsayyadim ("hunters") later in the verse; the Ketiv reads dawagim (or dogim) with the same meaning.
notes.17:8: Translates the Qere yir'eh (Qal imperfect of ra'ah, "see"), echoing 17:6 ("will not see when good comes"); the Ketiv yr' is understood as yira' ("fear," from yare').
notes.17:13: Translates the Qere wesuray ("and those who turn aside from Me"), from sur with a first-person singular suffix marking an abrupt shift to the LORD's voice; the Ketiv reads yswry.
notes.17:16: Hebrew lo-atsti mero'eh ahareka (Qal perfect of uts, "hurry," plus Qal participle of ra'ah, "shepherd") literally means "I have not hurried away from being a shepherd after You," and yom anush ("woeful day") uses the same root (anash, "incurable") as 15:18 and 17:9.
notes.17:19: Translates the Qere ha'am ("the people," with the definite article) in "the Gate of the Sons of the People"; the Ketiv reads am without the article.
notes.18:10: Ketiv reads the feminine ha-ra'ah, while Qere reads the masculine ha-ra' ("what is evil"), matching the standard Hebrew idiom for doing evil in God's eyes.
notes.18:14: Tsur saday uses the poetic singular noun saday ("open country / field"), and zarim ("foreign / distant") refers to cold streams flowing from distant mountain sources. Yinnateshu is Niphal imperfect of natash (elsewhere "be uprooted," cf. v. 7), used here of waters failing or drying up.
notes.18:16: Ketiv reads a variant singular spelling shrwqt, while Qere reads the plural construct sheriqot ("hissings of eternity," i.e., perpetual hissing).
notes.18:17: The Masoretic Text vocalizes er'em as Qal ("I will see them [with respect to] back and not face," i.e., seeing their back as they flee); revocalizing as Hiphil (ar'em) would yield "I will show them My back and not My face."
notes.18:23: Ketiv reads weqatal whyw ("and they will be"), while Qere reads jussive/imperfect weyihyu ("let them be"), continuing the preceding petitions. Mukhshalim is Hophal participle of kashal ("made to stumble"), echoing the Hiphil in v. 15.
notes.19:1: The Hebrew omits a verb before "some of the elders" by ellipsis; "take" is supplied to complete the command.
notes.19:2: Ketiv reads hchrswt, while Qere reads hacharsit ("the Potsherd Gate," linked to chares, "earthenware," in v. 1).
notes.19:7: Uvaqqoti (Qal weqatal of baqaq, "empty out / make void") creates a wordplay on baqbuq ("flask") in vv. 1 and 10.
notes.19:13: Vehassekh is a Hiphil infinitive absolute of nasakh continuing the finite verb qitteru ("burned incense"), a standard Biblical Hebrew syntactic construction.
notes.20:3: "Terror All Around" translates the symbolic Hebrew name Magor-missabib, which is immediately explained in v. 4 ("making you a terror") and echoed verbatim as a taunt in v. 10.
notes.20:7: Pittitani (Piel) and va-eppat (Niphal) come from the verb patah ("entice / persuade / deceive"), echoed in the Pual yefutteh in v. 10. Chazaqtani uses Qal of chazaq with a direct object suffix to mean "overpower / prove stronger than."
notes.20:12: "Inmost being and the heart" translates Hebrew kelayot va-lev (literally "kidneys and heart"), the biblical idioms for the seat of emotions and thought. Gilliti (Piel of galah, "uncover / lay open") pairs with rivi ("my legal case").
notes.20:17: Motetani (Polel of mut, "put to death") has a masculine singular subject referring back to the messenger of vv. 15-16, and merachem literally reads "from the womb" (i.e., while in the womb).
notes.21:2: The Hebrew spelling here and elsewhere in Jeremiah is Nebuchadrezzar, closer to the Babylonian form, rendered here with the standard English spelling Nebuchadnezzar.
notes.21:5: The Hebrew reverses the traditional Exodus formula of strong hand and outstretched arm into outstretched hand and strong arm, underscoring that the LORD Himself now fights against Jerusalem.
notes.21:9: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv reads the imperfect without waw, while the read qere translated here reads the weqatal form, meaning will live. Surrenders to renders the Hebrew idiom naphal al, literally falls upon or to, meaning to defect or surrender.
notes.21:12: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv reads their deeds with a third-person plural suffix, whereas the read qere translated here reads your deeds with a second-person plural suffix, matching the direct address in verses 12 and 14.
notes.22:4: The Hebrew shifts from plural kings to a distributive singular, he, his servants, and his people, viewing each succeeding Davidic king individually.
notes.22:6: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv reads a third-person feminine singular Niphal perfect treating cities collectively, whereas the read qere translated here reads the third-person plural Niphal perfect agreeing directly with plural cities.
notes.22:14: The unusual ending on hallonay, windows, likely reflects an archaic plural or dual form; paneled translates a Qal passive participle and coated translates a Qal infinitive absolute continuing the preceding finite verb.
notes.22:23: Ketiv/Qere: on both inhabit, a Qal participle, and nested, a Pual participle, the written ketiv preserves an archaic final i ending that the read qere omits. How pitiable you will be translates the Masoretic Niphal of hanan, to be pitied, though ancient versions read how you will groan from anah.
notes.22:24: The Hebrew shifts abruptly from third-person reference to Coniah to direct second-person singular address in tear you off, continuing into verses 25 and 26.
notes.23:2: Hebrew repeats the root paqad with contrasting senses across vv. 2 and 4: "cared for" (Qal), "hold accountable" (Qal with al, visit judgment upon), and in v. 4 "be missing" (Niphal).
notes.23:18: Translates the qere devaro ("His word"); the ketiv reads devari ("My word"). Hebrew sod denotes an intimate council or confidential assembly.
notes.23:26: The Masoretic clause "until when? Is there in the heart..." is syntactically elliptical, leaving the subject ("this" lying practice) implied.
notes.23:31: Hebrew vayyinamu neum uses the sole finite verb occurrence of naam in the Hebrew Bible together with its cognate noun neum ("declaration"), mocking the false prophets' imitation of the formula "declares the LORD."
notes.23:33: Hebrew massa carries a deliberate double sense throughout vv. 33-38, meaning both "prophetic oracle" and "burden." The Masoretic text reads et-mah-massa ("What burden?"), whereas the Septuagint and Vulgate redivide the consonants as attem hammassa ("You are the burden").
notes.23:39: The Masoretic vocalization reads Qal of nashah ("forget") with an infinitive absolute spelled with final aleph, creating an orthographic pun on nasa ("lift up") and massa ("burden"); the Septuagint and Vulgate read "lift up."
notes.24:8: Hebrew etten (Qal of natan, literally "I will give/make") introduces the comparison elliptically ("treat/render like"), which is then expanded by the same verb in v. 9 ("I will make them").
notes.24:9: Translates the qere lezaavah ("an object of terror/horror"); the ketiv reflects a metathesized form of the same noun with identical meaning.
notes.25:3: Hebrew ashkem is a variant spelling with initial aleph of the Hiphil infinitive absolute hashkem (as in v. 4); the idiom "rising early and..." expresses persistent, urgent action.
notes.25:7: Translates the qere hakhiseni (Hiphil infinitive construct with 1st-person suffix, "to provoke Me to anger"); the ketiv has a plural-like variant spelling.
notes.25:13: Translates the qere veheveti (Hiphil weqatal 1st-person singular of bo, "and I will bring"); the ketiv preserves an older variant spelling of the same form.
notes.25:14: In this text arrangement, the oracles against the nations begin immediately after 25:13 with the oracle concerning Elam (placed at 49:34-39 in the traditional Masoretic order).
notes.25:16: Translates the qere Elam ("Elam"); the ketiv reads olam ("forever/eternity"), an apparent scribal error for the nation's name.
notes.25:19: Translates both qere readings: ashiv (Hiphil of shuv, "I will restore") and shevut ("fortunes/restoration"); the ketiv reads Qal ashuv and shevit ("captivity").
notes.26:11: Ketiv writes the verb with an archaic 2fs ending (hrbyty), while the qere standardizes it to the Hiphil 2fs perfect hirbet, "you have multiplied."
notes.26:15: The noun "your mighty one" (abbireka) is morphologically plural, yet all three accompanying verbs and suffixes ("has been swept away," "did not stand," "thrust him down") are masculine singular, suggesting a collective or majestic plural referring to Pharaoh or Egypt's champion.
notes.26:20: The rare noun qeres ("gadfly") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, from a root meaning "to nip or pinch," fitting the heifer metaphor. The verb "has come" (ba') is doubled in the Masoretic text for urgency.
notes.26:25: Amon was the principal deity of No (Egyptian Thebes); similarly, Noph in 26:14 and 26:19 is the Hebrew name for Memphis.
notes.27:5: The verb "join yourselves" (nilwu) is a rare Niphal 2mp imperative retaining the n- prefix (parallel to "Come," Qal 2mp imperative), rather than a 1cp cohortative.
notes.27:6: Two ketiv/qere variants occur here: ketiv has singular hayah ("became") while qere reads plural hayu to match collective "My people," and ketiv has the adjective sobabim ("straying") while qere reads the Polel 3cp perfect with suffix sobebum ("they have turned them aside").
notes.27:11: Four verbs in this verse show ketiv 2fs forms addressing Babylon directly, whereas the qere reads 2mp forms ("you are glad," "you exult," "you prance," "and neigh") to agree with the plural vocative "pillagers of My inheritance" and 27:12.
notes.27:21: Merathaim (a Babylonian region) plays on the Hebrew root for "double rebellion," and Pekod (a tribe in Babylonia) plays on the Hebrew root paqad, "to punish/visit."
notes.27:29: The prepositional phrase "for her" (lah) is a qere w'lo ketiv (read in the Masoretic tradition though not written in the consonantal text); "archers" translates rabbim from the root rabab, "to shoot."
notes.27:44: Ketiv writes 'rwsm while qere vocalizes the Hiphil 1cs imperfect with suffix 'arisem ("I will make them run away"); the adverbial Hiphil form 'argi'ah means "in an instant."
notes.28:1: Leb-kamai literally means "the heart of those who rise against Me" and is a Hebrew Atbash cipher for Chaldea (Kasdim).
notes.28:2: Following the Masoretic vocalization, the noun means "foreigners," forming a wordplay with the following Piel verb "and they will winnow her" (repointed, the noun would read "winnowers").
notes.28:3: The written consonantal text (ketiv) duplicates the verb "bend," which the read tradition (qere) omits; the negative jussive particle is here vocalized with segol before the jussive verbs "bend" and the apocopated Hithpael "lift himself up."
notes.28:13: The ketiv preserves an archaic feminine singular participial ending, whereas the qere reads the standard feminine singular participle "you who dwell." The phrase "the measure of your cutting off" literally refers to the cubit-measure for cutting woven cloth from a loom, or alternatively "the measure of your unjust gain."
notes.28:19: Unlike the parallel in Jeremiah 10:16, the Hebrew text here omits "Israel" before "and of the tribe of His inheritance," connecting the phrase either to "the Former" or elliptically to Jacob.
notes.28:34: Five verbs in this verse have a ketiv/qere variant where the written text (ketiv) reads first-person plural suffixes ("us") and the read text (qere) reads first-person singular suffixes ("me"), aligning with the singular speaker Zion in verse 35. The final verb is vocalized from the Hiphil of the root for rinsing or flushing out rather than driving away.
notes.28:41: Sheshach is a Hebrew Atbash cipher for Babylon, parallel to Leb-kamai in verse 1.
notes.28:49: The Hebrew syntax is compressed ("also Babylon [is] to fall, the mortally wounded of Israel"), using the preposition plus infinitive construct to express inevitability ("must fall") in reciprocity for those killed because of Babylon.
notes.28:64: The Hebrew text retains "and they will grow weary," echoing the closing verb of verse 58 immediately before the editorial colophon concluding Jeremiah's words.
notes.29:3: The Hebrew nouns rendered "pounding" (sha'atah) and "feebleness" (ripyon) occur only here in the Hebrew Bible.
notes.29:5: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "their valley" ('imqam), referring to the Philistine coastal lowland, rather than the proper name "Anakites" reflected in the Septuagint.
notes.29:7: The Hebrew shifts abruptly from second-person feminine singular ("you be quiet") to third-person feminine singular ("it") in addressing and speaking about the sword.
notes.30:14: The Hebrew clause can also be construed with "the little ones of the flock" as the object ("they will drag them away, even the little ones of the flock") and the Hiphil verb yashim as transitive ("he will lay waste their pasture over them").
notes.30:17: Malcam (Hebrew malkam) is a form of the Ammonite deity Milcom's name and is identical in vocalization to "their king"; the reference to his priests in 30:19 confirms the deity.
notes.30:23: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv spells the king's name nbwkdr'swr (Nebuchadrezor), while the read qere followed here is Nebuchadrezzar, rendered with the standard English spelling Nebuchadnezzar.
notes.30:25: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv reads "against them" ('alehem), while the read qere followed here is "against you" ('alekem), matching the second-person plural earlier in the verse.
notes.30:29: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "on the sea" (bayyam), with masculine singular "it cannot" (yukal) referring back to the sea to portray restless agitation that cannot subside.
notes.30:31: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv is the standard feminine noun tehillah ("praise"), while the read qere followed here is tehillat, preserving an archaic feminine ending with the same meaning. The Masoretic Hebrew retains the negative "not" (lo) in this dramatic lament voiced for Damascus ("my joy").
notes.31:2: Hebrew wordplay pairs the town Heshbon with the verb hashebu ('they have plotted') and Madmen with tiddommi ('you will be silenced').
notes.31:9: Hebrew tsits elsewhere means 'blossom' or 'plate,' but here (with cognate support and the following verb) is widely understood as 'wings'; the verb phrase natso tetse pairs an unusual infinitive absolute from natsah ('fly') with a finite verb from yatsa ('go out').
notes.31:15: The clause weareha alah ('and one has gone up against her cities') pairs the feminine plural noun 'her cities' with a masculine singular Qal perfect verb alah ('has gone up'), rendered here with an impersonal subject, contrasting with yaredu ('have gone down') in the next clause.
notes.31:20: Translates the qere masculine plural imperatives helilu uzeaqu ('Wail and cry out'), matching the plural 'Declare' that follows; the ketiv reads feminine singular imperatives addressed to the city or land.
notes.31:41: Hebrew haqqeriyyot has the definite article and may denote either 'the towns' (paralleling 'the strongholds') or the Moabite city 'Kerioth' (cf. 31:24); both feminine plural subjects take singular feminine Niphal verbs (nilkedah, nitpasah).
notes.32:26: 'Sheshach' is a traditional Hebrew atbash cipher (reversing the alphabet) representing Babel (Babylon).
notes.32:30: Hebrew hedad ('harvest cry') refers to the rhythmic shout of grape-treaders in the winepress and is also used as a battle cry (cf. 31:33).
notes.32:34: Hebrew utephotekhem / utephotsotekhem ('and your dispersions') is a rare plural noun from the root puts ('scatter') with a second-person plural suffix, occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible.
notes.32:38: Hebrew haron hayyonah literally means 'the fierceness of the oppressing [one],' using the feminine Qal active participle of yanah ('oppress'), which elsewhere in Jeremiah modifies the feminine noun 'sword.'
notes.33:3: Note the threefold wordplay on the Hebrew root for evil or disaster (ra'ah/ro'a): 'evil way,' 'the disaster,' and 'the evil of their deeds.' The Niphal of nacham ('relent') is used consistently here and in vv. 13 and 19 for God withholding announced judgment.
notes.33:5: 'rising early and sending' renders two paired infinitives absolute (Hiphil hashkem and Qal shaloach), a recurring Jeremianic idiom expressing persistent, tireless action.
notes.33:6: Ketiv/Qere variant: the written ketiv has the extended feminine demonstrative form hazothah ('this'), while the read qere has the standard feminine demonstrative hazzoth ('this').
notes.33:18: Ketiv/Qere variant: the written ketiv reads 'Micaiah' (the longer theophoric spelling), whereas the read qere has the shorter form 'Micah,' followed here.
notes.34:8: 'until I have consumed them' translates the Qal infinitive construct of tamam with a 1st-person suffix and direct object ('my bringing an end to them'), a rare transitive use of a normally intransitive verb. The verb paqad ('punish' here with the preposition al) recurs in v. 22 with a direct object in the gracious sense 'attend to.'
notes.34:9: The Hebrew text explicitly reads 'your dreams' (chalomotheikhem) rather than 'your dreamers,' even though it appears in a list of human practitioners.
notes.34:11: Note the wordplay on the verb avad ('serve/work'): the nation that 'serves' the king of Babylon will be left on its land to 'cultivate' (literally 'work') it.
notes.34:18: The negation lebhilti ('so that ... not'), which normally governs an infinitive construct, is followed here by the finite 3rd-person plural perfect verb bo'u ('go').
notes.34:20: Ketiv/Qere variant: the written ketiv spells the king's name plene with a waw, while the read qere has the defective spelling without the waw (Jeconiah).
notes.35:1: Ketiv/Qere variant: the written ketiv has the construct form bishnath ('in the year of'), while the read qere has the definite absolute form bashanah ('in the [fourth] year'), agreeing with the definite adjective 'the fourth.'
notes.35:3: 'two full years' translates the Hebrew idiom shenatayim yamim (literally 'two years of days'; also in v. 11).
notes.35:8: The Hebrew text reads ra'ah ('disaster/calamity') rather than ra'abh ('famine'), which appears in the similar triad in 34:8.
notes.35:13: The Hebrew verb is 2nd-person masculine singular with penultimate stress (we'asitha, 'and you have made'), attributing the resulting iron yoke bars to Hananiah's own act of breaking the wooden bars, in contrast to God's 1st-person declaration in v. 14.
notes.35:16: 'sending you off' (Piel participle of shalach) creates an ironic wordplay with v. 15, 'The LORD has not sent you' (Qal perfect of the same root).
notes.36:8: Hebrew machlemim is a Hiphil participle with the second-person plural subject 'you,' understood either causatively ('that you cause to be dreamed,' i.e., solicit from your prophets) or as an internal Hiphil ('that you dream').
notes.36:14: Ketiv reads shevitchem ('your captivity'), whereas Qere reads shevutchem ('your fortunes/restoration'), forming the idiomatic expression shuv shevut ('restore the fortunes of,' also in 37:3, 18).
notes.36:21: The Hebrew here spells the king's name Nebuchadrezzar (closer to Akkadian Nabu-kudurri-usur), contrasting with Nebuchadnezzar in 36:1 and 36:3; vv. 21-22 also feature wordplay across Kolaiah (Qolayah), 'curse' (qelalah), and 'roasted them' (qalam).
notes.36:23: Ketiv reads hwyde' (a scribal transposition of yod and vav), whereas Qere reads hayyodea' (Qal active participle of yada' with the definite article, 'the one who knows').
notes.36:26: Peqidim ('overseers') is plural despite the singular address to Zephaniah, either stating a general office ('that there should be overseers') or including his fellow priests; tsinoq ('iron collar') is a biblical Hebrew hapax legomenon for a restraining neck-iron or pillory.
notes.37:8: Hebrew shifts abruptly from third person ('his yoke') to second person ('your neck... your bonds') and back to third person ('enslave him'), common in prophetic poetry; the idiom avad be- ('impose service on / enslave') contrasts with avad et- ('serve') in 37:9.
notes.37:13: The Masoretic pause (athnach) stands after lemazor ('for the sore,' traditionally linked to the first clause as 'for binding up'), though mazor ('sore/ulcer') pairs naturally with the medical phrase refuot te'alah ('remedies of healing').
notes.37:21: Hebrew arav et-libbo literally means 'pledged his heart' (Qal of arav, 'stand surety / give as a pledge'), an idiom for risking one's life or daring on one's own authority.
notes.37:23: Mitgorer is a Hithpolel participle (from garar, 'sweep/drag away,' hence 'a sweeping tempest'), contrasting with mitkholel ('whirling') in the parallel oracle at Jeremiah 23:19.
notes.38:21: Ketiv/qere variant: the written ketiv reflects an archaic second-person feminine singular spelling (homographic with the first-person singular), while the read qere is the standard second-person feminine singular Qal perfect of halakh ("you went").
notes.38:22: The Hebrew literally reads "a female surrounds a man" (Polel imperfect of savav, "encircle, encompass, protect"), an enigmatic proverb often understood as a surprising reversal of roles in which a woman protects or courts a warrior.
notes.38:32: The Hebrew Qal perfect ba'alti bam literally means "even though I was a husband/master to them," contrasting with Israel's breach of the covenant; the Septuagint reads "and I disregarded them" (cited in Hebrews 8:9).
notes.38:38: The word "coming" (Qal participle of bo') is a Masoretic qere without ketiv, supplied in the reading tradition though absent from the written consonantal text, matching the formula in 38:27 and 38:31.
notes.38:40: Ketiv/qere variant: the written ketiv (hasheremot) is an obscure, otherwise unattested form, while the read qere (hash-shedemot) means "the terraced fields" (compare 2 Kings 23:4).
notes.39:1: Ketiv reads the construct bishnat ("in the year of") before the definite ordinal, whereas Qere reads the absolute bashanah ("in the tenth year"); both convey the same date.
notes.39:9: Literally "seven shekels and ten of the silver," an additive Hebrew numeral construction meaning seventeen shekels of silver.
notes.39:12: MT reads dodi ("my uncle") here without ben ("son of"), unlike 39:7-9, where Hanamel is the son of Jeremiah's uncle; dod can also denote a kinsman more broadly.
notes.39:23: Ketiv reads the plural ("Your laws"), whereas Qere reads the singular ("Your law"); the Hiphil wayyiqtol wattaqre ("You caused to befall") is spelled with final aleph from the root qara II (equivalent to qarah, "happen, befall").
notes.39:35: The Hiphil infinitive construct leha'avir literally means "to cause to pass over" (without "through the fire" in the Hebrew text here), an idiom for child sacrifice to Molech.
notes.40:2: The Hebrew uses three feminine singular object suffixes ("it") with no explicit antecedent in the Masoretic text, variously understood as the earth, Jerusalem, or the LORD's decree.
notes.40:3: The Qal passive participle betsurot literally means "fortified" or "walled off," used metaphorically for inaccessible things beyond human reach.
notes.40:5: The terse Hebrew connects directly to 40:4: the third-person plural suffix on the Piel infinitive construct lemal'am ("to fill them") refers back to the demolished houses of Jerusalem.
notes.40:6: The noun ateret ("abundance") is a biblical hapax legomenon, related to the root atar ("be rich, abundant").
notes.40:8: Ketiv and Qere are purely orthographic (plene versus defective) spelling variants of the same form, "for all."
notes.41:3: The clause "his mouth will speak with your mouth" renders the Hebrew idiom literally, using the preposition et ("with") to express a direct face-to-face encounter.
notes.41:5: The noun misrefot ("burnings") and verb yisrefu ("make a burning") refer to the royal funerary custom of burning aromatic spices in honor of a deceased king (cf. 2 Chr 16:14; 21:19).
notes.41:11: Ketiv reads a Hiphil form (wayyakhbishum, causative "made them subject"), whereas Qere reads the Qal wayyikhbeshum ("and subdued them"), matching the Qal verb in 41:16; the translation follows the Qere.
notes.41:17: Ketiv writes the noun with transposed middle consonants (lezo'ah/lezawa'ah), whereas Qere reads leza'awah ("an object of horror"); both convey the same sense, and the translation follows the Qere.
notes.41:18: Hebrew plays on two repeated verbs: karat ("cut") for both making a covenant and cutting the calf in two, and abar ("pass/transgress") for both transgressing the covenant and passing between the calf's parts. Literally "the calf" lacks a comparative preposition and functions as a double accusative with natan ("make [them like] the calf"), with the verb resumed in 41:20.
notes.42:6: The Hebrew text alternates between the shorter spelling Jonadab (42:6, 10, 19) and the longer spelling Jehonadab (42:8, 14, 16, 18) for the same Rechabite ancestor.
notes.42:14: The Hophal singular verb huqam ("have been upheld") governs a plural logical subject introduced by the object marker et, an impersonal passive construction in Biblical Hebrew. The paired infinitives absolute hashkem wedabber ("rising early and speaking," and similarly hashkem weshaloaḥ in 42:15) are a characteristic Jeremianic idiom for earnest, persistent action.
notes.42:15: Hebrew contrasts two similar-sounding Qal imperatives: shuvu ("turn back," from shuv) at the start of the prophetic message and ushevu ("then you will dwell," from yashav), an imperative expressing the promised consequence of repentance.
notes.42:17: Unlike 42:13, 18, and 19 ("the LORD of hosts"), the Hebrew here reads the fuller title "the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel."
notes.43:2: Hebrew megillat-sepher literally means "scroll of a book" (or document); this chapter distinguishes megillah ("scroll") from sepher ("book").
notes.43:7: Hebrew tippol techinnatam liphne literally reads "their supplication will fall before," an idiom for humbly presenting a plea for favorable reception (also in 44:20).
notes.43:16: Hebrew pachadu 'ish 'el-re'ehu literally means "they dreaded, each toward his companion," a pregnant construction expressing that they turned to one another in dread.
notes.43:22: Hebrew we'et-ha'ach lephanaw mebo'aret places the marker 'et before the grammatical subject ha'ach ("the brazier") with the feminine Pual participle mebo'aret ("burning, kept alight").
notes.43:23: Hebrew delatot literally means "doors," used as a scribal term for the rectangular columns of text on a scroll; wehashlekh is a Hiphil infinitive absolute continuing the iterative action of the preceding verb.
notes.44:4: Translated according to the Qere hakkelu' ("the prison," from kala', "restrain, shut up"); the Ketiv is an orthographic variant spelling h-k-l-y-'.
notes.44:10: Hebrew meduqqarim is the Pual participle of daqar ("pierce through"), referring to soldiers critically wounded in battle.
notes.44:12: Hebrew lachaliq is a difficult form, usually taken as a defective Hiphil infinitive construct of chalaq ("divide, apportion") meaning to obtain a share of property or produce; some derive it from a homonymous root meaning "to slip away."
notes.44:16: Hebrew bet habbor literally means "house of the cistern" (a subterranean dungeon), and hachanuyot is a hapax legomenon denoting vaulted subterranean cells or chambers.
notes.44:19: Translated according to the Qere we'ayyeh ("and where [are]...?"), agreeing with plural "your prophets"; the Ketiv reads w-'-y-w (we'ayyo, "and where is he?"), bearing a third-person masculine singular suffix.
notes.45:2: Ketiv reads the Qal imperfect יחיה ("will live"), whereas Qere reads the waw-consecutive Qal perfect וְחָיָה ("will live"), marking the apodosis after the participial subject.
notes.45:11: Ketiv includes the definite article on the second noun of the construct chain (הסחבות), whereas Qere omits the article (סְחָבוֹת, "worn-out rags"), matching the indefinite בְּלוֹיֵי מְלָחִים that follows.
notes.45:16: Ketiv writes the object marker את before אֲשֶׁר; this is a ketiv velo qere (written but not read) and is omitted in the Qere.
notes.45:23: The Masoretic vocalization תִּשְׂרֹף is Qal 2ms active ("you will burn"), holding Zedekiah directly responsible for the city's burning (contrast the Niphal passive תִּשָּׂרֵף in 45:17).
notes.45:28: The closing clause וְהָיָה כַּאֲשֶׁר נִלְכְּדָה יְרוּשָׁלִָם (lit. "And it came about when Jerusalem was captured") stands in the MT as an abrupt transitional clause linking to the capture account in chapter 46.
notes.46:1: The Hebrew spelling here is נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּר ("Nebuchadrezzar"), rendered with the standard modern English spelling "Nebuchadnezzar."
notes.46:3: "Rab-saris" (lit. "chief officer/eunuch") and "Rab-mag" are transliterated Babylonian court titles; the translation follows the MT word divisions סַמְגַּר־נְבוּ ("Samgar-nebo") and שַׂר־סְכִים ("Sarsechim").
notes.47:3: Ketiv reads indefinite דבר, whereas Qere supplies the definite article הַדָּבָר ("this thing") in agreement with the demonstrative הַזֶּה.
notes.47:5: The clause וְעוֹדֶנּוּ לֹא־יָשׁוּב וְשֻׁבָה (lit. "And while he had not yet turned back, and go back...") shifts abruptly from a 3ms narrative aside into Nebuzaradan's direct imperative with the verb of speaking implied.
notes.47:8: Ketiv reads עופי ("Ophai"), whereas Qere reads עֵיפַי ("Ephai").
notes.47:14: "To strike you dead" renders the Hebrew idiom לְהַכֹּתְךָ נָפֶשׁ (Hiphil infinitive construct of נָכָה with adverbial accusative נֶפֶשׁ, lit. "to strike you as to life"; likewise יַכֶּכָּה נֶּפֶשׁ in 47:15).
notes.47:16: Ketiv writes the short jussive form תעש, whereas Qere reads the full form תַּעֲשֵׂה (both Qal 2ms of עָשָׂה, "do," with the same sense after אַל).
notes.48:1: The phrase "and the chief officers of the king" (werabbe hammelekh) is syntactically ambiguous in the MT, either governed by the preceding preposition "from" as part of Ishmael's own status or listing additional companions who came with him.
notes.48:7: The clause "slaughtered them into the middle of the cistern" (wayyishhatem el-tokh habbor) uses a pregnant construction, compressing the acts of slaughtering the men and casting their bodies into the cistern.
notes.48:9: The MT phrase "on account of Gedaliah" (beyad-Gedalyahu) reads literally "by the hand of Gedaliah," an unusual idiom understood here as "on account of" or "alongside" Gedaliah.
notes.48:17: The Ketiv reads kmwhm while the Qere reads kimham ("Chimham"). Geruth (gerut) is a hapax legomenon from the root gur ("sojourn"), meaning "lodging place," functioning here with Chimham as a place name.
notes.49:6: The Ketiv reads the unique biblical form anw while the Qere standardizes it to classical anahnu, both meaning "we."
notes.49:10: The construction shov teshvu pairs an abbreviated infinitive absolute (resembling shuv, "return," but serving here for yashav, "stay") with the Qal imperfect of yashav for emphasis ("if you will indeed stay").
notes.49:20: The Ketiv reads ht'tym while the Qere reads hit'etem (Hiphil perfect 2mp of ta'ah, "lead astray / practice deceit"), combined with benafshoteikhem ("at the cost of your own lives," using the preposition be of price).
notes.50:9: The noun melet ("mortar") is a hapax legomenon, and malben (from levenah, "brick") here denotes a brick pavement or terrace at the palace entrance.
notes.50:10: The Ketiv reads shprwrw while the Qere reads shafrirw, a hapax legomenon meaning "his royal canopy" or "pavilion." The 1cs Qal perfect tamanti ("that I have hidden") attributes Jeremiah's prophetic sign-act directly to the LORD, and the Hebrew spells the king's name Nebuchadrezzar.
notes.50:11: The Ketiv reads wb'h while the Qere reads uva (Qal perfect 3ms with vav-consecutive of bo, "and he will come").
notes.50:12: The MT shifts directly from the 1cs Hiphil wehitstati ("I will kindle," spoken by the LORD) to 3ms verbs referring to Nebuchadnezzar. The Qal verb atah literally means "wrap oneself in" or "put on," portraying Nebuchadnezzar's effortless domination of Egypt.
notes.50:13: The "pillars" (matstsevot) of Beth-shemesh ("House of the Sun") refer to the monumental obelisks of the Egyptian sun-temple city of Heliopolis.
notes.51:4: The paired infinitives absolute (Hiphil of shkm and Qal of shlh, literally 'rising early and sending') form a recurring Jeremianic idiom for persistent, earnest action.
notes.51:9: Hebrew literally has a third-person masculine singular suffix on 'wives' ('his wives'), used distributively for each of the kings of Judah (or collectively referring back to Judah); it is smoothed here to 'their wives.'
notes.51:19: Hebrew leha'atsivah is a Hiphil infinitive construct of the verb 'tsb ('shape, form') with a third-person feminine singular suffix, referring to shaping sacrificial cakes in the likeness of the queen of heaven.
notes.51:25: The Hebrew alternates between second-person feminine plural verbs ('spoken,' 'confirm,' 'carry out') and masculine plural suffixes ('your mouths,' 'your hands,' 'your vows'), highlighting the joint participation of both the Judean men and their wives.
notes.51:34: The closing Hebrew clause is notably terse (literally 'and [object marker] all the land/earth it is'), specifying the full scope of the LORD's tearing down and uprooting; Hebrew erets can mean either 'the land' or 'the earth.'
notes.52:1: Translated from the qere (read form) Hamutal; the ketiv (written form) spells the name Hamital.
notes.52:11: Translated from the qere, which omits the preposition 'in' before 'house' (using an adverbial accusative of place), whereas the ketiv writes 'in the house of'; Hebrew beit-happequddot ('house of custody') is a unique term for a place of detention.
notes.52:20: The Masoretic Hebrew literally reads 'that were under the stands,' whereas 1 Kings 7:25 locates the twelve bronze oxen under the sea (and the Septuagint adjusts accordingly).
notes.52:21: Translated from the qere construct form 'the height of the one pillar'; the ketiv reads the absolute noun 'in height.'
notes.52:23: Hebrew ruchah (literally 'toward the wind') refers to the pomegranates exposed on the outer sides of the capital's latticework.
notes.52:31: Translated from the qere 'the house of confinement' (Qal passive participle of kl' 'confine'); the ketiv reads an orthographic variant of the same noun for prison.
notes.52:32: Translated from the qere 'the kings' (with the definite article); the ketiv omits the definite article ('kings').

unplaced.text: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying:
And you will speak all these words to them, yet they will not listen to you; and you will call to them, yet they will not answer you.
And they have treated the wound of the daughter of My people lightly, saying, "Peace, peace," yet there is no peace.

Were they ashamed because they committed an abomination? No, they were not ashamed at all, and they did not know how to feel disgrace. Therefore they will fall among those who fall; at the time of their punishment they will stumble, says the LORD.
There is no one like You, LORD; great are You, and great is Your name in might.
Who would not fear You, King of the nations? For to You it is due, because among all the wise of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is no one like You.
And altogether they are senseless and foolish; the instruction of worthless things—it is wood.
unplaced.note: Hebrew habalim, literally "vanities" or "empty breaths," refers here to worthless idols.

unplaced.text: Yet the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and the eternal King. At His wrath the earth trembles, and nations cannot withstand His indignation.
For I solemnly warned your fathers on the day I brought them up from the land of Egypt, and up to this day, rising early and warning, saying, "Listen to My voice."
unplaced.note: The Hebrew idiom "rising early and warning" conveys persistent, earnest admonition.

unplaced.text: The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point; it is engraved on the tablet of their heart and on the horns of your altars,
unplaced.note: MT shifts here from third-person "their heart" to second-person plural "your altars."

unplaced.text: while their children remember their altars and their Asherah poles beside a leafy tree, on the high hills.
My mountain in the field, your wealth, all your treasures, I will give for plunder—your high places, because of sin throughout all your borders.

And you will relinquish—by your own doing—your inheritance that I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for you have kindled a fire in My anger; it will burn forever.
unplaced.note: MT reads literally "and in you," indicating Judah forfeits its inheritance by its own doing.

unplaced.text: For many nations and great kings will enslave them as well, and I will repay them according to their deeds and according to the work of their hands.

And I will give them into the hand of those who seek their life, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants; and afterward she will be inhabited as in former days, declares the LORD.
Come out from her midst, My people, and let each one rescue his life from the burning anger of the LORD.

And do not let your heart grow faint or be afraid because of the report heard in the land: a report will come in one year, and after it in the following year another report, and violence will be in the land, and ruler against ruler.
Therefore, look, days are coming when I will punish the carved images of Babylon, and all her land will be put to shame, and all her fatally wounded will fall in her midst.
And heaven and earth and all that is in them will shout for joy over Babylon, for from the north the destroyers will come against her, declares the LORD.
Yet afterward I will restore the fortunes of the sons of Ammon, declares the LORD.

In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stood without strength, for fire went out from Heshbon and a flame from the midst of Sihon, and it devoured the brow of Moab and the crown of the head of the sons of tumult.
Woe to you, Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished, because your sons have been taken into captivity and your daughters into exile.
But I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the last days, declares the LORD. Up to this point is the judgment on Moab.
At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying:
unplaced.note: MT reads "Jehoiakim" here, though the ensuing oracle is set in the reign of Zedekiah.

unplaced.text: And all the nations will serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the time of his own land comes as well; and many nations and great kings will enslave him.
Why should you die, you and your people, by the sword, by famine, and by plague, just as the LORD has spoken concerning the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon?
Do not listen to them. Serve the king of Babylon and live. Why should this city become a wasteland?
For this is what the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, says concerning the vessels that remain in the house of the LORD, and in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem:
For this is what the LORD says regarding the king who sits on the throne of David, and regarding all the people living in this city, your brothers who did not go out with you into exile:
This is what the LORD of hosts says: Look, I am sending the sword, the famine, and the plague against them, and I will make them like disgusting figs that cannot be eaten because they are so bad.

I will pursue them with the sword, the famine, and the plague, and I will make them an object of dread to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, a horror, a hissing, and a disgrace among all the nations where I have banished them,
because they did not listen to My words, declares the LORD, when I sent My servants the prophets to them, rising early and sending—yet you did not listen, declares the LORD.
unplaced.note: MT shifts abruptly from third person ("they") to second person plural ("you").

unplaced.text: As for you, listen to the word of the LORD, all you exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon.

As for you, do not be afraid, My servant Jacob, declares the LORD, and do not be dismayed, Israel; for look, I am going to save you from far away, and your seed from the land of their captivity. Jacob will return and be at rest and secure, with no one to terrify him.

For I am with you, declares the LORD, to save you; for I will bring complete destruction upon all the nations where I have scattered you, yet I will not bring complete destruction upon you. I will discipline you with justice, and I will certainly not leave you unpunished.
Why do you cry out over your wound? Your pain is incurable. Because of the abundance of your iniquity, since your sins are so many, I have done these things to you.
And you will be My people, and I will be your God.
Look, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will carry out the good word that I spoke to the house of Israel and to the house of Judah.
In those days and at that time I will make a branch of righteousness sprout for David, and he will administer justice and righteousness in the land.
In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will live securely; and this is what she will be called: "The LORD Is Our Righteousness."
unplaced.note: MT uses the feminine pronoun here, applying this title directly to the city of Jerusalem.

unplaced.text: For this is what the LORD says: David will never be without a man sitting on the throne of the house of Israel,
and the Levitical priests will never be without a man in My presence offering burnt offerings, burning grain offerings, and preparing sacrifices for all time.
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, saying:
This is what the LORD says: If you can annul My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night, so that day and night do not come at their proper time,
then My covenant may also be annulled with My servant David, so that he will not have a son reigning on his throne, and with the Levitical priests, My ministers.
Just as the host of the heavens cannot be counted and the sand of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the seed of My servant David and the Levites who minister to Me.
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, saying:

Have you not noticed what these people have spoken, saying, "The two families that the LORD chose, He has rejected"? And they treat My people with contempt, so that they are no longer a nation before them.
This is what the LORD says: If My covenant with day and night does not stand, and if I have not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth,

then I will also reject the seed of Jacob and of My servant David, so as not to take rulers from his seed over the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and show compassion to them.

When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the fighting men saw them, they fled and went out from the city by night along the way of the garden of the king, through the gate between the two walls, and he went out toward the Arabah.
unplaced.note: MT shifts from plural ("they") to singular ("he"), focusing on King Zedekiah.

unplaced.text: Then the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. They captured him and brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he pronounced judgment against him.
Then the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes at Riblah, and the king of Babylon also slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.
He also put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in bronze shackles to bring him to Babylon.
The Chaldeans burned the house of the king and the house of the people with fire, and they tore down the walls of Jerusalem.
Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard exiled to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, the deserters who had defected to him, and the rest of the people who remained.
unplaced.note: MT repeats "the rest of the people" in both clauses.

unplaced.text: But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left behind in the land of Judah some of the poor people who had nothing at all, and on that day he gave them vineyards and fields.
Now Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave orders concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, saying:
"Take him and watch over him, and do not do anything harmful to him; rather, just as he speaks to you, so deal with him."
So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officials of the king of Babylon sent word.
unplaced.note: Rab-saris and Rab-mag are Babylonian court titles.

unplaced.text: What came as the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet regarding the nations.
And he did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD, according to everything Jehoiakim had done.
For on account of the LORD's anger this happened in Jerusalem and Judah until He cast them away from His presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard deported some of the poorest of the people, the rest of the people who remained in the city, the defectors who had defected to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen.
unplaced.note: The Hebrew term rendered "craftsmen" refers to skilled artisans, though some understand it as a variant spelling for "populace" or "multitude" as in 2 Kings 25:11.

unplaced.text: These are the people whom Nebuchadnezzar deported: in the seventh year, three thousand twenty-three Judeans;
unplaced.note: Hebrew spells the king's name Nebuchadrezzar here and in the following two verses, a variant of Nebuchadnezzar.

unplaced.text: in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, eight hundred thirty-two individuals from Jerusalem.
In the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard deported seven hundred forty-five Judean individuals. Altogether, there were four thousand six hundred individuals.
